rows.historical_meaning: Irish dath (colour, hue); colour named directly as the thing itself, before any judgment is passed on it.

rows.definition: One turn of the earth, and the span a life is lived in units of. Also, in this house, one continuous stretch that may run far past a date.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Old English dæg named the turning itself, not the clock that later divided it, and this house's own stretched use of the word sits closer to that old sense than to any calendar square. A day here can outlast the date it started on, because the word was never really bound to the date at all.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English dæg (day), from Proto-Germanic *dags; one turn of the earth, and by extension the unit a life is counted in.

rows.definition: Short form of database. A structured store built for retrieval.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Short form of database. A structured store built for retrieval, kept under a name small enough to type quickly.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin data (things given) + Greek βάσις (basis, foundation), clipped in modern usage to the two letters db; the same structured store built for retrieval, only shortened to fit a name.

rows.definition: A compound fragment naming a database check. Not an English word; flagged for the mis-cut band.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: It is not a word with a history, only two abbreviations pushed together where a longer name was cut short. What it names is the check it performs, and nothing more is recoverable from the fragment itself.

rows.definition: To take a thing out of running while leaving it present. Deactivation is not removal.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To take a thing out of running while leaving it present. What it undoes is the activity, never the thing's existence.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin de- (down, away, reversal) + activus (active), from agere (to do, drive, act); to take a thing out of running while leaving its presence intact, reversal without removal.

rows.definition: To ignore repeats that arrive too fast to be meant. It waits for the trembling to settle before answering.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The bounce it removes is a mechanical shudder, not a decision — a switch settling before it means what it says. Debouncing trusts stillness over speed: the first signal is not answered until it stops repeating itself.
rows.historical_meaning: English de- (reversal) + bounce (Middle English bounsen, to knock, strike, likely imitative); to ignore repeats that arrive too fast to be meant, waiting for a signal's own trembling to settle before answering it.

rows.definition: To find why a thing behaves other than intended. Debugging is the disciplined narrowing of where the truth differs from the belief.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The bug it removes is an old word for a flaw, older than any insect ever found in a machine — debugging was never really about an animal, only about a defect worth naming plainly. What is found this way is always a gap between what was believed and what was actually there.
rows.historical_meaning: English de- (reversal, removal) + bug (a flaw in a mechanism, attested from the 1870s, well before the often-repeated moth story of the 1940s); to find why a thing behaves other than intended, narrowing where belief and truth diverge.

rows.definition: The digits after the point. Decimals state precision and say nothing about accuracy.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The digits after the point. Decimals state precision, and precision alone — they say nothing at all about whether the number is actually accurate.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin decimalis (of a tenth part), from decimus (tenth), from decem (ten); the digits set after the point, stating precision about a number without saying anything about its accuracy.

rows.definition: A choice made, closing the others. A decision is only real once something becomes impossible.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: A choice made, closing off the others. It is only real the moment something else becomes genuinely impossible, not merely less preferred.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin decisio (a cutting off, decision), from decidere (to cut off, decide), from de- (off) + caedere (to cut); a choice made by cutting the other options away, real only once something has become impossible.

rows.definition: A full ordered set of cards, and a flat raised surface. Both are things laid out ready to be used.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Dutch root is a covering, a roof laid flat over something else, and both later senses kept that flatness. A deck of cards and a ship's deck are each a surface laid out for whatever happens on top of it.
rows.historical_meaning: Middle Dutch dec (a covering, roof), related to English thatch; a flat covering surface, extended to a full ordered set of cards laid out ready on such a surface.

rows.definition: A statement made openly and on the record. A declaration binds the one declaring, which is what separates it from a remark.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin clarus is clear, and a declaration's root promise is a clarity strong enough to be held to later. A remark can be walked back; a declaration is a statement made with that door already closed.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin declaratio (a making clear, declaration), from declarare (to make fully clear), from de- (thoroughly) + clarare (to clarify), from clarus (clear, bright); a statement made openly enough to bind the one who makes it.

rows.definition: To read the meaning back out of the coded — reversal of encoding, faithfully.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To read the meaning back out of the coded. It is the faithful reversal of encoding, recovering exactly what was put in rather than reinterpreting it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin de- (reversal) + codex (book, later a system of symbols), from caudex (tree trunk, block of wood used for writing tablets); to read the meaning back out of a coded form, faithfully reversing what encoding did.

rows.definition: That which turns an encoded form back into what it carried. Decoding recovers; it does not interpret.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root, codex, is a wooden tablet a code was once written on, and a decoder still only reverses that writing, never adds to it. What comes out the other side is exactly what went in, restored rather than explained.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin de- (reversal) + codex (a system of symbols, from caudex, a wooden writing tablet); that which turns an encoded form back into what it carried, recovering rather than interpreting.

rows.definition: What is added for delight rather than for function. Decoration is not waste — it is where a made thing says it was cared about.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its Latin root, decere, is about fittingness before it is about beauty — a decoration is judged by whether it belongs, not only by whether it pleases. What earns a place this way was made by someone who stayed past what the function required.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin decoratio (an adorning, decoration), from decorare (to beautify, adorn), from decor (grace, beauty, from decere, to be fitting); what is added for delight rather than for function, marking that a made thing was cared for beyond mere necessity.

rows.definition: To remove repeated copies so each thing is counted once. Deduplication is how an archive stops lying about its size.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is doubling undone — duplicare folded a thing into two, and deduplication unfolds it back to one. An archive that has not been unfolded this way is always larger on paper than it is in fact.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin de- (reversal) + duplicare (to double), from duplex (twofold, from duo, two + plicare, to fold); to remove repeated copies so each distinct thing is counted only once.

rows.definition: Extending far inward. Of what is not reached by a surface look.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Extending far inward. Of whatever a surface look alone could never reach.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English deop (deep, profound), from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, related to dive; extending far inward, past whatever a surface glance could reach.

rows.definition: A named model lineage this house has worked with. A named system rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The compound reads as an instruction before it reads as a name — go deep, and keep seeking — and the house keeps it as a proper name rather than translating the instruction back out of it. What it names is worn here, not defined.
rows.historical_meaning: Modern English compound of deep (Old English deop, extending far inward, as in deep learning) + seek (Old English secan, to search for); a company and model-lineage name coined in the 2020s, worn as a proper name rather than glossed further.

rows.definition: Short form of define, and of definition. A named abbreviation rather than a concept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Short form of define, and of definition. A named abbreviation rather than a concept of its own, standing in for the drawing of a boundary around a meaning.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin definire (to bound, limit, define), from de- (thoroughly) + finire (to bound, finish), from finis (boundary, end); clipped in code and speech to def, a shortened stand-in for define or definition.

rows.definition: What holds when nothing is chosen. A decision made in advance, on behalf of whoever does not decide.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Old French root is a failing, not a fallback — a default was first the gap left by a missing choice, and only later the answer quietly standing in that gap. What holds by default was decided by someone else, in advance, for exactly the moment a choice never arrives.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French defaute (a failing, lack), from defaillir (to fail, be lacking), from Latin de- (away) + fallere (to deceive, fail); what holds when nothing else was chosen, a decision made in advance on behalf of whoever fails to choose.

rows.definition: To state what a thing is, tightly enough to exclude what it is not. To define is to draw a boundary around a meaning.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its Latin root, finis, is an ending — to define a thing is to decide, in advance, where it stops being itself. A meaning drawn without that edge has not yet been defined, only described.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin definire (to limit, determine, define), from de- (thoroughly) + finire (to bound, end), from finis (boundary); to state what a thing is by drawing a boundary tight enough to exclude what it is not.

rows.definition: A statement of what a thing is, drawn tightly enough to exclude what it is not. To define is to set a boundary around a meaning.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin finis is an ending, and a definition inherits that: it draws the line where a word's meaning stops, not only where it starts. A boundary that cannot say what falls outside it has not defined anything yet.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin definitio (a boundary, definition), from definire (to bound, determine); a statement of what a thing is, drawn tightly enough that what it is not falls plainly outside it.

rows.definition: Loss of quality by stages rather than all at once. Graceful degradation means less is offered rather than nothing.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root, gradus, is a rank on a ladder, and degradation was first about falling a rung, not falling off entirely. A system built to degrade gracefully loses rank one step at a time, never all its rungs at once.
rows.historical_meaning: Medieval Latin degradatio (a reduction in rank), from degradare (to reduce in rank), from de- (down) + gradus (step, rank); loss of quality taken down by stages rather than all at once, one step lost at a time.

rows.definition: A named power in a pantheon — in this house's architecture, the Greek names the realms wear (Athena's library, Hermes' bazaar): organizing spirits, never objects of worship.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Latin root, deus, carries a shine — an old word for the sky's own brightness before it ever named a single god. This house borrows the shine as a label for its rooms and never asks the label to be believed in.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin deitas (godhood, divinity), from deus (god), from Proto-Indo-European *deiwos (heavenly, shining); a named power in a pantheon, borrowed here as an organizing spirit rather than an object of worship.

rows.definition: Time deliberately or unavoidably placed between two events. A delay can be a fault or a mercy.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Time deliberately or unavoidably placed between two events. Whether it reads as a fault or a mercy depends entirely on who needed the gap.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French delaier (to put off, defer), from de- (intensive) + laier (to leave, allow, related to laisser); time placed deliberately or unavoidably between two events, which can be either a fault or a mercy depending on who needed the gap.

rows.definition: The handing of authority to another to act in one's place. Delegation transfers the doing and never the answering for it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin lex, law, sits inside the root — a delegation was always a legal appointment, not a favor granted informally. What travels with that appointment is the doing alone; the law never lets the answering for it travel with it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin delegatio (an assignment, delegation), from delegare (to send on a commission, entrust), from de- (down, away) + legare (to appoint by law, from lex, law); the handing of authority to another to act in one's place, transferring the doing while the answering for it stays put.

rows.definition: To remove entirely, at the owner's word. Bound in this house by the purge law: when deletion is asked, it is complete — and it is never asked lightly.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The image underneath is a wax tablet wiped smooth, not a page torn out — deletion was first about a surface returned to blank, with nothing left to read even where the marks used to be. What this house completes when asked leaves that same clean surface behind.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin delere (to destroy, blot out), likely from de- (away) + linere (to smear, daub), the sense of wiping a wax tablet clean; to remove entirely, at the owner's word, and to leave nothing where the thing once stood.

rows.definition: To carry a thing to where it belongs and leave it standing there — arrival as a promise kept.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root is freeing, not transporting, Latin liberare, to set loose — to deliver something was first to release it, only later to carry it somewhere specific. Arrival, in the oldest sense of the word, was always also a letting-go.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French delivrer (to free, deliver), from Late Latin deliberare (to liberate), from Latin de- (thoroughly) + liberare (to free), from liber (free); to carry a thing to where it belongs and set it loose there, arrival as a kind of freeing.

rows.definition: A showing meant to prove rather than describe. A demo ends an argument by being watched.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its root, monstrum, once named an omen strong enough to need no argument behind it. A demo keeps that force: it settles a question by being seen, not by being explained.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin demonstrare (to point out, show fully), from de- (thoroughly) + monstrare (to show), from monstrum (a portent, sign), clipped in modern usage to demo; a showing meant to prove rather than merely describe.

rows.definition: A showing that proves rather than describes. A demonstration ends an argument by being watched.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: It shares demo's root in monstrum, an omen strong enough to need no argument, at full length rather than clipped. What a demonstration proves, it proves by being witnessed directly, the same way an omen was never argued for, only seen.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin demonstratio (a pointing out, proof), from demonstrare (to show fully), from de- (thoroughly) + monstrare (to show), from monstrum (a sign, portent); a showing that proves rather than describes, ending an argument by being witnessed directly.

rows.definition: To repeat data on purpose so it is faster to read. Denormalising trades one truth for many copies of it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Norma is a carpenter's square, the tool a rule is checked against, and denormalizing deliberately sets that tool aside for speed. Every copy made this way is a small bet that none of them will ever need to disagree.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin de- (reversal) + normalis (made according to a rule), from norma (a carpenter's square, rule, pattern); to repeat data on purpose so it reads faster, trading a single truth for several copies of it.

rows.definition: How much is packed into a given space. Density decides how much attention a surface asks for.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin densus is crowded, and density was first a word about closeness, not about weight — how near things stand to each other inside a fixed space. A crowded surface asks more of the eye than a sparse one holding the same amount.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin densitas (thickness, density), from densus (dense, thick, crowded); how much is packed into a given space, deciding by that packing how much attention the space will demand.

rows.definition: A thing another thing cannot work without. Every dependency is a place where someone else's choices reach you.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: It shares dependents' root of hanging from something else, but names the thing hung upon rather than the thing doing the hanging. Every choice made inside a dependency is a choice made, at a distance, for whatever relies on it.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin dependere (to hang from, depend on), from de- (down, from) + pendere (to hang); a thing another thing cannot work without, named for hanging down from whatever it relies on.

rows.definition: Those that rely on another to work. Every dependent is a place a change reaches further than intended.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin pendere is to hang, and a dependent is still hanging in that literal sense, suspended from something else's continued standing. Move what it hangs from, even slightly, and the motion travels all the way down.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin dependere (to hang from), from de- (down, from) + pendere (to hang); those that hang from, and so rely on, another thing to work.

rows.definition: To put a made thing into the place where it will actually run. Deployment is where a build meets reality.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Old French root is an unfolding, not a placing — a deploy takes something folded up in preparation and opens it into the shape it will actually run in. Everything before that moment stays folded, however finished it looks.
rows.historical_meaning: Old French desploiier (to unfold), from Latin displicare (to scatter, unfold), from dis- (apart) + plicare (to fold); to put a made thing into the place where it will actually be unfolded and run, past all rehearsal.

rows.definition: That which puts a made thing where it will actually run. Deployment is where a build meets reality.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Where deploy names the unfolding, a deployer is the hand that does it, the agent rather than the act. It carries a build across the last gap between finished and running.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin displicare (to unfold, scatter), from dis- (apart) + plicare (to fold); that which puts a made thing where it will actually run, unfolding it out of rehearsal and into use.

rows.definition: The putting of a made thing where it will actually run. Deployment is where a build meets reality.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The putting of a made thing where it will actually run. It is where a build meets reality, and nothing about a plan is truly tested before this.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin displicare (to unfold, scatter), from dis- (apart) + plicare (to fold); the putting of a made thing where it will actually run, the unfolding out of rehearsal into use.

rows.definition: The marking of a thing as no longer preferred, before removing it. Deprecation is a warning given in advance so nothing breaks unannounced.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Latin root is a prayer said to ward something off, not a command to remove it — deprecation asks a thing to fall out of use, it does not force the fall. The removal, when it comes, was announced long before it arrived.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin deprecatio (a warding off by prayer, deprecation), from deprecari (to pray against, avert by entreaty), from de- (away) + precari (to pray, beg); the marking of a thing as no longer preferred, a warning given ahead of its removal.

rows.definition: How far a thing extends inward or downward. Depth is what a surface conceals.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Old English root is an adjective made into a measure, depth being simply deep turned into a number. What that number reports is always distance the eye cannot reach from where it is standing.
rows.historical_meaning: Old English deop (deep), with the abstract noun suffix -th; how far a thing extends inward or downward, exactly what a surface glance conceals.

rows.definition: The chain by which one thing came from another. A derivation is what makes a result checkable rather than merely asserted.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Latin image is a channel cut from a river, not an assertion made from nothing — a derivation is a path a claim travelled, and the path can be walked back. What has no such channel has to be taken on trust instead.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin derivatio (a diverting, drawing off), from derivare (to divert a stream), from de- (away, from) + rivus (a stream); the chain by which one thing was drawn off from another, tracing a path a claim can be checked against.

rows.definition: To obtain one thing from another by a traceable path. Derivation is what makes a result checkable.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: It is derivation's own verb, the drawing-off itself rather than the channel left behind by it — Latin rivus, a stream, diverted rather than dammed. What is derived can always be traced back upstream to what it was diverted from.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin derivare (to divert a stream, draw off), from de- (away, from) + rivus (a stream); to obtain one thing from another along a traceable path, the way a channel is drawn off from a river.

rows.definition: To say what a thing is like. Description reports and does not instruct — reading one as an instruction is a common error.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: The Latin root is a copy made by writing something down, not an order given — describere records a shape, it does not command one. Treating a description as a set of steps mistakes a report for a recipe.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin describere (to write down, sketch, copy), from de- (down) + scribere (to write); to say what a thing is like, reporting its shape rather than instructing what should be done about it.

rows.definition: To take a thing out of what was chosen. Deselection restores an option that had been closed.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin legere is to gather, and deselecting ungathers one thing from a set without touching anything else still held. It restores exactly one closed door, and no others.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin de- (reversal) + seligere (to choose apart, select), from se- (apart) + legere (to choose, gather); to take a thing back out of what was chosen, restoring an option that had been closed off.

rows.definition: Deciding the shape of a thing before it is made. Design is where most of a thing's fate is settled.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin signum is a mark, and design was first the marking-out of a plan, a line drawn before any material touched it. Most of what a made thing becomes was already decided in that mark, long before the making itself began.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin designare (to mark out, designate), from de- (thoroughly) + signare (to mark), from signum (a sign, mark); deciding the shape of a thing before it is made, marking out its plan in advance of the making.

rows.definition: A computer meant to stay in one place, and the surface its interface imitates. Named for the furniture it replaced.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Its own name is a small joke on furniture: a desktop is the screen standing in for the wooden surface a desk once was, borrowed word and all. What moved across into the screen was the metaphor, not the disc the deeper root once meant.
rows.historical_meaning: English compound of desk (Medieval Latin desca, from Latin discus, a disc, platter) + top (Old English topp, summit); a computer meant to stay on that surface, and the interface built to imitate the furniture it replaced.

rows.definition: Where a going is aimed. A destination gives a journey its shape without being most of it.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: Latin stare is to stand, and a destination was first something made to stand firm, fixed before the journey begins, so the journey has something to aim at rather than merely wander. Fixing the end this way is what turns motion into a route.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin destinatio (a fixing, appointment), from destinare (to make firm, determine), from de- (thoroughly) + stare (to stand); where a going is aimed, fixed in advance of the journey that will reach it.

rows.definition: A small part attended to on its own. Detail is where a general claim either holds or fails.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: French tailler is to cut, and a detail is a piece severed from the whole precisely so it can be examined alone. A claim too coarse to survive being cut this way was never as solid as its general shape suggested.
rows.historical_meaning: French détail (a cutting into pieces), from détailler (to cut up), from de- (apart) + tailler (to cut), from Late Latin taliare (to cut); a small part attended to on its own, cut apart from the whole to be examined closely.

rows.definition: To notice what was there but unnoticed. Detection finds; it does not create.
rows.sanctuary_meaning: To notice what was there but unnoticed. Detection finds what already existed; it never creates what it reports.
rows.historical_meaning: Latin detegere (to uncover, expose), from de- (reversal) + tegere (to cover); to notice what was already there but covered over, uncovering rather than creating anything new.
